Designing a repeatable microservice scheduling experiment

What to control, what to measure, and what to record when comparing policies under changing conditions.

Two scheduling policies can appear to disagree simply because they experienced different workloads or network conditions. A repeatable experiment makes those conditions explicit so that the comparison is easier to interpret.

Define the scenario before comparing policies

Start with the application, workload, infrastructure, and behavior you want to study. Record what changes, when it changes, and which conditions remain fixed across policy runs.

  • Application version, deployment configuration, and resource requests.
  • Request rates, request mix, replay duration, and workload generation settings.
  • Network delay, bandwidth settings, topology, and the timing of changes.
  • Policy settings, initialization, measurement windows, and run order.

Check that the intended conditions actually happened

A configured delay is an input to the emulation mechanism. The delay experienced by an application is a measurement. Validating the relationship between them is part of evaluating the experimental environment.

The same applies to bandwidth limits and workload generation. If an intended input is not achieved, the experiment may still produce a result, but it answers a different question from the one originally posed.

Measure the application and the mechanism

InputsWorkloads, network conditions, deployment state, and policy settings.
MechanismTelemetry, emulation accuracy, decision behavior, and scheduling overhead.
OutcomesResponse time, throughput, successful requests, and resource behavior.

Application response time describes what users experience. Scheduler overhead and migration behavior help explain how the policy produced that result. Emulation accuracy helps establish what environment the policy was actually tested in.

Preserve enough context to repeat the comparison

Keep configuration, code versions, raw observations, analysis scripts, and the interpretation of each metric together. Repeating a run is most useful when the next reader can understand both the experiment and the conditions attached to its conclusions.

Reproducibility is a property of the complete experimental workflow: the scenario, the mechanism, the measurements, and their recorded context.

These concerns motivate iDynamics, a framework for evaluating microservice scheduling under controllable cloud–edge dynamics. See the paper and implementation for the research framework.
